classes.tooltip:
The built-in flight controller: velocity (PID, world frame) -> thrust vector and attitude ->
attitude (P on the quaternion error) -> body rates (PI with inertia feed-forward) -> thrust
allocation over the rotors. Each mode enters the cascade at its own level. The default gains suit
the default airframe at 1 kHz.

classes.tooltip:
Flight controller of a physics multirotor. The multirotor calls Compute Motor Commands once per
physics step (or every Controller Rate Divider steps) with the ground-truth state and the setpoint
of the active control mode, and applies the normalized motor commands it returns.

Subclass it in C++ (override the _Implementation functions) to bring your own controller. A
Blueprint subclass works too, but runs at the physics rate (1 kHz by default) through the
Blueprint VM; raise Controller Rate Divider for it.

Rigid-body multirotor for flight-control research: rotors with motor lag, thrust and reaction
torque, air-relative drag and gravity, integrated in fixed steps on uBot sim time. A flight
controller turns the active command into motor commands, or motor commands drive the rotors
directly. Accepts velocity (heading frame), attitude, body-rate and motor commands.

properties.tooltip: Mass, inertia, rotors and drag. Changes take effect at the next Reset Flight.
What the drone does when its commands stop: released by the sender, or older than Command Timeout Seconds.
Commands older than this (sim time) count as lost, s. 0 leaves the timeout to the sender (uBot ROS components have their own).
The controller runs every this many physics steps and its commands are held in between.

Flight controller for velocity, attitude and body-rate commands. Replace it with your own subclass.

classes.tooltip:
Flies the owning multirotor with keyboard or gamepad while a local player controls (possesses) it.
The input actions and the mapping context are created at run time (Enhanced Input), so no assets
are needed; set your own to change the keys. While it controls the drone it sends a command every
frame. When control ends, it depends on the Flight Mode: in Velocity mode the drone brakes and hovers;
in Angle and Rate mode the attitude command is released, and the drone's Command Loss Action decides
what happens next (Hover by default).

properties.tooltip: Your own mapping context; it must map Custom Move Action and Custom Yaw Action. Empty uses the built-in keys.
Your own move action (Axis3D: forward, right, up), used with Custom Mapping Context.
Your own yaw action (Axis1D, + yaws right), used with Custom Mapping Context.
Stick dead zone, share of full deflection.

classes.tooltip:
Base of the multirotor flight models. Moves the root component (the updated component) in fixed
physics steps on uBot sim time, sweeps its collision shape through the world and slides along what
it touches (the ground is a surface like any other), and presents the pose extrapolated to the
current sim time every frame. Accepts velocity commands
(IUBotVelocityCommandable) in the heading frame: X forward and Y right along the current heading,
Z up; only the Z angular velocity (yaw rate) is used.

Implements IUBotBodyStateSource for its updated component: the state is the integrator's at the latest
physics step (the component shows it extrapolated to the current sim time), so sensors can read it, and
no physics backend can bind the same body.

properties.tooltip: Actuator id reported to uBot. Empty uses the robot id of the owner (its uBot Identity, else its name).
Sliding friction on contact: the sliding speed drops by this share of the impact speed.

properties.displayName: Impact Event Min Speed Meters Per Second
properties.tooltip: Impacts slower than this (along the surface normal) do not fire On Impact, m/s.
At most this many physics steps per frame. When a frame is longer, the extra time is skipped and a warning is logged once.
Physics steps per second of sim time. More steps are more accurate and cost more.
Velocity commands above these limits are clamped.

classes.tooltip:
Simplified flight control for navigation research: the drone tracks velocity commands with a
smooth, bounded response (first order, limited acceleration and jerk) and brakes to a stop within
a bounded distance. There are no forces or attitude dynamics; the tilt follows the acceleration.
